content_voiceover: This table is a high-yield reference on Taiwanese hemoglobin variants, which show up on boards as classic exam bait. Notice the pattern: most of these are stable hemoglobins found incidentally, causing no clinical disease, like Hb G-Taichung, Hb Kaohsiung, and Hb J-Meinung, which is actually the most common variant in Taiwan at just over one percent. The key testable concept is distinguishing stable variants from the ones that actually cause disease. Hb Köln and Hb Perth are unstable hemoglobins that precipitate as Heinz bodies and cause chronic hemolysis. Hb S and Hb C are the classic variants tested worldwide, both from beta-6 glutamate substitutions, valine for sickle disease and lysine for the milder Hb C disease. Finally, remember that HbE and Hb Constant Spring are not simple variants at all, they behave as thalassemic hemoglobins, meaning they pair with alpha or beta thalassemia mutations to produce clinically significant thalassemia syndromes. That distinction between a silent variant, an unstable variant, and a thalassemic variant is the core concept examiners want you to apply.
keypoints: Most Taiwanese Hb variants are clinically silent, stable Hb
Hb J-Meinung (β56Gly→Asp) = most common TW variant, ~1%
Hb Köln, Hb Perth = unstable Hb → Heinz bodies, hemolysis
Hb S (β6Glu→Val) and Hb C (β6Glu→Lys) = African variants
HbE and HbCS behave as thalassemic Hb variants, not silent
keypoint_voiceover: Key points here: most Taiwanese hemoglobin variants are stable and clinically silent, with Hb J-Meinung being the most common at about one percent. Unstable variants like Hb Köln and Hb Perth cause Heinz body hemolysis. Hb S and Hb C are the classic beta-6 substitutions from African populations. And critically, HbE and Hb Constant Spring are not silent, they act as thalassemic hemoglobin variants.
